sources.title: LFCA Program Changes
sources.notes: DISPUTED. States 'The LFCA domains will remain unchanged but please review the upcoming changes to competencies... which are outlined below each domain heading.' Two problems, both verified in a browser on 2026-08-09. (1) No per-domain change outlines exist on the page; whole-page text is 2,556 characters and stops at the 22 competency names. (2) The claim that domains are unchanged is contradicted by the Linux Foundation's own archived certification page (see wayback-lfca-2025-08): all six domain weights changed, and the domain 'Supporting Applications and Developers' (8%) was renamed to 'IT Project Management Fundamentals' (10%). This project records the archived evidence rather than the page's claim, and documents the disagreement here rather than silently choosing.

sources.title: Linux Foundation Certified IT Associate (LFCA)
sources.notes: Canonical current syllabus. The Domains & Competencies accordion is JS-rendered and requires a browser, but it contains only domain names, weights and the 22 competency names: fully expanding it adds zero characters (container text is 1,930 characters either way, verified 2026-08-09). This is the basis for recording competency name as the finest published objective granularity.

sources.title: Fundamentals of Open Source IT and Cloud Computing (LFS200) — course content

sources.title: proc_pid_oom_score_adj(5) — Linux manual page
sources.notes: As of 2026-08-11 this page still documents a badness-score factor removed from the kernel in commit d46078b28889 and absent from mm/oom_kill.c since Linux 4.17: "root processes are given 3% extra memory over other tasks." The guide's own Traps paragraph for sysadmin.troubleshooting.out-of-memory-and-the-oom-killer already states this correctly ("that bias was removed in Linux 4.17, although proc_pid_oom_score_adj(5) still documents it"); this source record backs that claim, which the previous man-proc-pid-oom-score record (a different page) did not carry.

sources.title: Linux kernel Documentation/filesystems/proc.rst
sources.notes: Actively maintained in-tree kernel documentation. Section 3.1 covers /proc/<pid>/oom_adj and /proc/<pid>/oom_score_adj; unlike the man-pages project's proc_pid_oom_score_adj(5) page, it does not repeat the removed 3% root-process bonus.

sources.title: RFC 2644 / BCP 34: Changing the Default for Directed Broadcasts in Routers
sources.notes: Updates RFC 1812. Changes the required router default for directed-broadcast receipt and forwarding from permit to block. RFC 919 (1984) alone, previously the sole cited source for this concept's broadcast-forwarding claim, predates this default change by 15 years and is not authority for any modern router default.

sources.title: Default outbound access in Azure
sources.notes: States that the Azure portal already defaults new subnets to private, and that in the API version released after 2026-03-31, defaultOutboundAccess for subnets in new VNETs defaults to false across ARM templates, PowerShell and CLI too — contradicting the older claim that outbound reachability is an inherent, unrouted property of an Azure virtual network.

sources.title: SANS Institute: Incident Response (glossary) — the six-step PICERL framework
sources.notes: States verbatim: "SANS Incident Response Framework: Details a tactical six-step process encompassing Preparation, Identification, Containment, Eradication, Recovery, and Lessons Learned." This is the PICERL sequence previously cited only to nist-sp-800-61r3, which no revision of NIST SP 800-61 has ever published — Rev. 2 used a four-phase life cycle and Rev. 3 (April 2025) reorganised around six CSF 2.0 Functions (Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover), a different list.

sources.title: What is Multicloud? Multicloud Explained
sources.notes: Defines multicloud ("the use of at least two CSPs at once") and explicitly contrasts it with hybrid cloud, matching this concept's confused_with pairing. Added alongside nist-sp-800-145, which was previously the sole source despite never mentioning multi-cloud — kept because the concept's own pedagogical point is that multi-cloud is conspicuously absent from NIST's four deployment models.

sources.title: SP 800-77 Rev. 1: Guide to IPsec VPNs
sources.notes: Defines a VPN as a secure virtual network built on physical infrastructure; §2.4.2 describes the remote-access architecture in which a host establishes an encrypted IPsec tunnel to a gateway and can then use organizational resources as though attached to the private network.

sources.title: RFC 9111: HTTP Caching
sources.notes: Defines an HTTP cache as a local store of response messages that reduces response time and bandwidth by reusing prior responses, and formalizes the freshness/staleness distinction central to the concept.

sources.title: RFC 6349: Framework for TCP Throughput Testing
sources.notes: Formally defines Bottleneck Bandwidth (capacity), RTT (delay/latency), and TCP Throughput (achieved rate), and the Bandwidth-Delay Product relation that explains why a high-bandwidth, high-RTT link underperforms its nominal rate.

sources.title: OASIS Advanced Message Queuing Protocol (AMQP) Version 1.0
sources.notes: Conceptual model defines queues as nodes that 'store and forward messages' between producers and consumers, named as separate application elements -- the queue as buffer decoupling them.

sources.title: OMG Unified Modeling Language (OMG UML), Version 2.5.1 - Clause 18, Use Cases
sources.notes: Clause 18.2.5.1 defines a UseCase as actions performed in collaboration with Actors yielding an observable result of value; 18.1.3.1 states a UseCase can include variations including exceptional behavior and error handling.

sources.title: Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN), Version 2.0.2 - Clause 10, Process; Clause on Lane/Pool
sources.notes: Clause 10.1 defines a Process as a sequence/flow of Activities carried out to do work; the Lane/Pool constructs are the notation mechanism for making hand-offs between participants visible on the diagram.

sources.title: Using a Three-Tier Architecture Model - Win32 apps
sources.notes: Defines the presentation, business/middle, and data tiers as separately deployable services, and states the three-tier approach supports scalability and relocating components independently.

sources.title: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook (NASA SP-2016-6105 Rev2)
sources.notes: Cited for three concepts. §4.2.1.2.2 defines functional requirements as 'what functions need to be performed to accomplish the objectives.' Appendix C ('How to Write a Good Requirement') defines writing requirements clearly, completely, consistently and traceably. Appendix B (Glossary) gives adjacent definitions of Verification ('did I build the product right?') and Validation ('am I building the right product?').

sources.title: What is MoSCoW Prioritization?
sources.notes: First-party definition of MoSCoW (Must/Should/Could/Won't Have) from the consortium that originated and stewards the scheme.

sources.title: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook, Section 6.2 - Requirements Management
sources.notes: States that requirements management maintains bidirectional traceability 'between stakeholder expectations, customer requirements, technical product requirements, product component requirements, design documents, and test plans and procedures.'

sources.title: Standard Glossary of Terms Used in Software Testing, Version 2.2
sources.notes: Cross-references user acceptance testing to acceptance testing, defined as testing 'with respect to user needs ... to enable the user, customers or other authorized entity to determine whether or not to accept the system' (after IEEE 610).

sources.title: NASA Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) Handbook, NASA/SP-2016-3404/REV1
sources.notes: Defines the WBS as a hierarchical, product-oriented 'family tree' subdivided into manageable segments, and defines Work Packages as units of work assigned to a single organizational element with a budget/value and scheduled dates -- small enough to estimate and assign.

sources.title: Ansible Glossary -- Idempotency
sources.notes: Defines idempotency: an operation is idempotent if the result of performing it once is exactly the same as the result of performing it repeatedly without intervening actions.

sources.title: Security Considerations in the System Development Life Cycle (SP 800-64 Rev. 2)
sources.notes: Section 3 enumerates and defines the SDLC phases (initiation, development/acquisition, implementation/assessment, operations/maintenance, disposal), mapping onto requirements through maintenance.

sources.title: Site Reliability Engineering, Chapter 12: Effective Troubleshooting
sources.notes: Cited for three concepts. Lays out report/observe, hypothesize, test (Diagnose/Test and Treat), fix (Cure), and write-up (documentation) steps; describes bisection/divide-and-conquer for narrowing scope; and states that 'reproducing [a problem] at will' is how a causal factor is proven.

sources.title: Site Reliability Engineering, Chapter 11: Being On-Call
sources.notes: States the on-call engineer 'triage[s] the problem and work[s] toward its resolution, possibly involving other team members and escalating as needed,' and names clear escalation paths as a core on-call resource.

sources.title: User Story Template for Agile | Agile Alliance
sources.notes: States the 'As a... I want to... So that...' template: role who wants to accomplish something, what they want to accomplish, and why.

sources.title: What is a Minimum Viable Product (MVP)? | Agile Alliance
sources.notes: Defines an MVP as the 'version of a new product which allows a team to collect the maximum amount of validated learning about customers with the least effort.'

sources.title: PostgreSQL Documentation: SQL Commands
sources.notes: One-line canonical definitions for SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE; JOIN is documented as a clause of SELECT rather than a standalone statement.

sources.title: PostgreSQL Documentation: UPDATE
sources.notes: States that UPDATE 'changes the values of the specified columns in all rows that satisfy the condition' and shows WHERE as an optional clause in the synopsis, which is the primary support for the fact that an UPDATE with no WHERE clause acts on every row. Added during Task 40 verification because postgresql-sql-commands, the source previously cited for that fact, is an index of command names and does not state it.

sources.title: Microservices architecture style - Azure Architecture Center
sources.notes: States that services 'can be deployed independently', that 'microservices are responsible for persisting their own data or external state', and that they 'communicate through well-defined APIs', with messaging frameworks named for asynchronous communication. Added during Task 40 verification because cncf-glossary, the source previously cited alone, defines microservices as independent services but says nothing about per-service data ownership or the interfaces between them.

sources.title: What is NoSQL?
sources.notes: Enumerates key-value, document, graph, and wide-column NoSQL families and states the schema/scale trade-off against relational ACID guarantees.

sources.title: Beginner's Guide
sources.notes: Describes serving static files as a web-server task, and routing requests to FastCGI servers 'which run applications' as the application-server half of the pair.

sources.title: About pull requests
sources.notes: Defines a pull request as a proposal to merge code changes where authors and reviewers discuss the change and the Checks tab shows automated tests, builds, and other validations.

sources.title: Introduction to the Dependency Mechanism
sources.notes: Defines Maven's dependency mechanism as resolving a project's application-level library dependencies. Registered for a language-agnostic concept because no npm or pip first-party page made the application-vs-OS package manager contrast explicit; see PROGRESS.md known-weakness note.

sources.title: Amazon EBS snapshots
sources.notes: States EBS snapshots are point-in-time copies stored in Amazon S3, separate storage from the source volume that survives its deletion -- confirming the cloud-snapshot half of the concept's description.

sources.title: About Azure Spot Virtual Machines
sources.notes: States Azure evicts Spot VMs 'with 30-seconds notice,' delivered on a best-effort basis via Azure Scheduled Events, with a Deallocate (default) or Delete eviction policy and no hibernate option -- registered to correct a cycle-3 finding that AWS's 2-minute Spot interruption mechanics were stated in the guide's generic 'the provider' voice as if universal to spot/preemptible pricing.

sources.title: Preemptible VM instances / Spot VMs
sources.notes: States 'the shutdown period for a preemption notice is best effort and up to 30 seconds,' delivered via an ACPI G2 Soft Off signal, with no hibernate option -- registered alongside azure-spot-vms to correct the same cycle-3 finding.

sources.title: CNCF Cloud Native Glossary: Function as a Service (FaaS)
sources.organization: Cloud Native Computing Foundation / Linux Foundation
sources.notes: States 'Charges apply solely for the duration of computation, ensuring no costs accrue when functions are inactive,' distinguishing FaaS from models like PaaS 'which require continuous resource availability,' and that a function instance is 'initiated per request and terminated post-execution.' Registered because the guide's serverless-and-faas concept attributed this claim to the CNCF serverless glossary page, which does not contain it -- a citation-mismatch defect found in cycle 3. Tier 1 to match cncf-glossary, cncf-charter and cncf-who-we-are: CNCF sits under the Linux Foundation, the certifying body, so its own glossary is tier 1 in this dataset (see the pre-existing cncf-glossary-serverless and cncf-glossary-virtualization records, tier 2, for the inconsistency this does not attempt to fix).

sources.title: CNCF Cloud Native Glossary: Container
sources.organization: Cloud Native Computing Foundation / Linux Foundation
sources.notes: States 'Containers share the same operating system and its machine resources, spreading the operating system's resource overhead' and 'Since containers share the same operating system, processes can be considered less secure than alternatives.' Registered because the guide's container-vs-virtual-machine concept attributed these claims to the CNCF virtualization glossary page, which never mentions containers -- a citation-mismatch defect found in cycle 3. Tier 1, matching cncf-glossary/cncf-charter/cncf-who-we-are per the same rationale as cncf-glossary-faas above.

sources.title: What are AWS Cost and Usage Reports?
sources.notes: States 'You can customize the AWS Cost and Usage Reports to aggregate the information either by the hour, day, or month,' supporting the guide's cost-monitoring claim that providers expose cost and usage data at daily, sometimes hourly, granularity. Registered because that claim was previously cited to aws-budgets (the AWS Budgets page), which discusses Budgets' own refresh cadence and notification lag, not the underlying data's time granularity -- a citation-mismatch (source-cited-for-content-it-does-not-contain) defect found in cycle 3, the seventh confirmed instance of this class across two cycles.

sources.title: Six advantages of cloud computing
sources.notes: First of the six advantages: 'Trade fixed expense for variable expense -- Instead of having to invest heavily in data centers and servers before you know how you're going to use them, you can pay only when you consume computing resources, and pay only for how much you consume.' Registered to replace aws-rightsizing-whitepaper as the source for the capex-vs-opex concept: that whitepaper is entirely about instance rightsizing and contains no CapEx/OpEx accounting material at all, a citation-mismatch defect found in cycle 3. This page uses 'fixed expense' / 'variable expense' rather than the accounting terms 'capital expenditure' / 'operational expenditure,' but is the same distinction the guide's prose describes -- an up-front, sized-for-peak cost versus a pay-per-consumption cost.

sources.title: Availability - AWS Well-Architected Framework, Reliability Pillar
sources.notes: Defines availability as "the percentage of time that a workload is available for use", calculated over a period, gives the nines table, and shows the calculations for hard dependencies and for independent redundant components. Added 2026-08-17 by the Performance/Availability verification pass, which found the availability items cited the Reliability Pillar welcome page, whose entire text is an abstract and a list of the six pillars.

sources.title: Site Reliability Engineering, Appendix A: Availability Table
sources.notes: Tabulates allowed unavailability per availability level: 99.9% is 43.2 minutes per 30 days and 99.95% is 21.6 minutes per 30 days. Added 2026-08-17: the downtime arithmetic item cited Chapter 4 (SLOs), which carries no such table.

sources.title: REL11-BP02 Fail over to healthy resources - AWS Well-Architected Framework
sources.notes: States that failover means moving to healthy resources in unimpaired locations, that a read replica must be promoted and traffic then pointed at the new endpoint, and that detection sensitivity is an anti-pattern to weigh. Added 2026-08-17 for the failover and high-availability items.

sources.title: REL11-BP03 Automate healing on all layers - AWS Well-Architected Framework
sources.notes: States that "a best practice is to make services stateless where possible. This prevents loss of data or availability on resource restart" and that Auto Scaling "can perform self-healing on stateless applications". Added 2026-08-17 as the stateless-design source; the items previously cited the Reliability Pillar welcome page.

sources.title: REL11-BP05 Use static stability to prevent bimodal behavior - AWS Well-Architected Framework
sources.notes: States that the capacity needed after a zone loss must already have been provisioned before the failure, so the workload operates in a single mode. Added 2026-08-17 for the N+1 provisioning item.

sources.title: REL11-BP07 Architect your product to meet availability targets and uptime SLAs - AWS Well-Architected Framework
sources.notes: States that a published availability target or uptime SLA has to be supported by the architecture and operational processes, and that a workload should account for its dependencies' own SLAs. Added 2026-08-17 for the SLA-versus-architecture item.

sources.title: REL10-BP01 Deploy the workload to multiple locations - AWS Well-Architected Framework
sources.notes: States that workload data and resources should be distributed across multiple Availability Zones or Regions, and that a fundamental principle is to avoid single points of failure "including the underlying physical infrastructure". Added 2026-08-17 for the redundancy/failure-domain item.

sources.title: What is an Application Load Balancer?
sources.notes: States that an Application Load Balancer "functions at the application layer, the seventh layer of the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model" and routes on the content of the application traffic. Added 2026-08-17: the layer-4-versus-layer-7 item cited the ELB overview page, which never names either layer.

sources.title: What is a Network Load Balancer?
sources.notes: States that a Network Load Balancer "functions at the fourth layer of the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model" and forwards to a target using the protocol and port specified. Added 2026-08-17 as the transport-layer half of the load-balancer-layer item.

sources.title: Configure sticky sessions for your Classic Load Balancer
sources.notes: States that a load balancer "routes each request independently to the registered instance with the smallest load" by default, and that the sticky session feature "enables the load balancer to bind a user's session to a specific instance" so all requests in that session go to the same instance. Added 2026-08-17 for the sticky-sessions item.

sources.title: Change the instance type of an Amazon EC2 instance
sources.notes: States that "you must stop your instance before you can change its instance type" and to "plan for downtime while your instance is stopped". Added 2026-08-17: the vertical-scaling items cited the EC2 Auto Scaling page, which is about horizontal scaling and never mentions resizing an instance.

sources.title: Values specific for simple records (TTL) - Amazon Route 53
sources.notes: Defines TTL as the time "that you want DNS recursive resolvers to cache information about this record" and states that a longer TTL means "it takes longer for changes to the record (for example, a new IP address) to take effect". Added 2026-08-17 for the DNS-failover delay item.

sources.title: Manage how long content stays in the CloudFront cache (expiration)
sources.notes: States that CloudFront serves a file from an edge location until the configured cache duration passes, then forwards the next request to the origin to check for a newer version, and that infrequently requested files may be evicted before expiry. Added 2026-08-17 for the cache-staleness item.

sources.title: Multi-AZ DB instance deployments - Amazon RDS
sources.notes: States that Amazon RDS provides high availability and failover support by maintaining a synchronous standby replica in a different Availability Zone, and describes the failover as an event the service performs. Added 2026-08-17 as the worked example behind the redundancy-plus-failover items.

sources.title: Site Reliability Engineering, Chapter 6: Monitoring Distributed Systems
sources.notes: States that "the four golden signals of monitoring are latency, traffic, errors, and saturation", defines saturation as how full the service is against its most constrained resource, and warns that a mean latency hides the tail ("with an average latency of 100 ms at 1,000 requests per second, 1% of requests might easily take 5 seconds"), recommending latency histograms. Added 2026-08-17: the golden-signals, percentile and saturation items all cited the AWS pillars landing page, whose whole text is a list of the six pillars.

sources.title: NIST CSRC Glossary: fault tolerance
sources.notes: Defines fault tolerance as "a property of a system that allows proper operation even if components fail" -- proper operation continuing through the failure, and bounded to the components the design covers. Added 2026-08-17 for the fault-tolerance items.

sources.title: Implement observability - AWS Well-Architected Framework, Operational Excellence Pillar
sources.notes: States that "observability goes beyond simple monitoring, providing a comprehensive understanding of a system's internal workings based on its external outputs" and that it is "rooted in metrics, logs, and traces". Added 2026-08-17 for the monitoring-versus-observability item.

sources.title: Kinesis Producer Library concepts: aggregation
sources.notes: States that aggregation stores multiple records within a single stream record and "allows customers to increase the number of records sent per API call, which effectively increases producer throughput", with the worked example of packing 1,000 records into 10. Added 2026-08-17 as the documented half of the batching throughput/latency trade.

sources.notes: Documents the busy condition (open files, a working directory inside the mount, a swap file in use) and the semantics and caveats of the lazy unmount -l.

sources.title: fuser(1) — identify processes using files or sockets
sources.notes: Documents -m NAME, which lists all processes accessing files on the mounted filesystem containing NAME — the standard way to find what is holding a busy mount open.

sources.title: symlink(7) — symbolic link handling
sources.notes: Defines hard links as indistinguishable references to one file and defines a dangling symbolic link as one naming a pathname that does not exist.

sources.title: link(2) — make a new name for a file
sources.notes: Documents EXDEV: oldpath and newpath are not on the same mounted filesystem — the error behind a hard link refusing to cross a filesystem boundary.

sources.title: du(1) — estimate file space usage
sources.notes: Summarizes device usage of a set of files by walking the directory tree, which is what makes space with no remaining name invisible to it.

sources.title: mkswap(8) — set up a Linux swap area
sources.notes: States that after creating the swap area you need swapon(8) to start using it, and that swap areas are usually listed in /etc/fstab so swapon -a takes them into use at boot.

sources.title: swapon(8) — enable devices and files for paging and swapping
sources.notes: Documents activating a swap device directly, --show, and the separate role of the /etc/fstab swap entries used by swapon -a.

sources.title: lvm(8) — LVM2 logical volume manager
sources.notes: States that a Volume Group is a collection of one or more Physical Volumes and that each block of an LV is stored on one or more PV in the VG, and lists the resize commands (lvextend, lvreduce, lvresize, pvmove).

sources.title: resize2fs(8) — ext2/ext3/ext4 filesystem resizer
sources.notes: States it can enlarge or shrink an unmounted filesystem, and that a mounted filesystem can only be expanded — the source for ext4 shrink being an offline-only operation.

sources.title: xfs_growfs(8) — expand an XFS filesystem
sources.notes: States the filesystem must be mounted to be grown, and that shrinking is limited to the last allocation group ("Only shrinking the last AG without removing it is implemented").

sources.title: sysctl.d(5) — configure kernel parameters at boot
sources.notes: States that at boot systemd-sysctl.service reads /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf and writes each key to the corresponding path under /proc/sys — the mechanism that makes a runtime sysctl change persist.

sources.title: proc_sys(5) — the /proc/sys sysctl pseudo-filesystem
sources.notes: Describes /proc/sys as files corresponding to kernel variables that can be read and in some cases modified through the /proc filesystem.

sources.title: vmstat(8) — report virtual memory statistics
sources.notes: Defines si and so as the amount of memory swapped in from and out to disk per second — a rate, as distinct from the standing swap-used level that free(1) reports.

sources.title: md(4) — Multiple Device driver (Linux software RAID)
sources.notes: Describes RAID0/1/4/5/6/10 as implemented by the md driver: RAID5 distributes parity across all devices and survives one device failure; RAID1 members hold exactly the same data written in parallel; RAID6 needs N+2 drives for N drives of data. Added 2026-08-18 (cycle 3, verify-sysadmin-e) — the raid-levels concept previously cited proc(5), which says nothing about RAID.

sources.title: Managing RAID — RAID levels and linear support (RHEL 9)
sources.notes: States that RAID level 4 and 5 require at least 3 disks, that RAID 5's storage capacity is calculated the same way as level 4 (all but one drive), that RAID 1 capacity equals the smallest mirrored member, and that RAID 10 can be built from 3 drives (1.5x the smallest device). Added 2026-08-18 (cycle 3, verify-sysadmin-e).

sources.title: crontab(1) — maintain crontab files for individual users
sources.notes: Documents that user crontabs live in /var/spool/ but "are not intended to be edited directly", that -e installs the modified crontab automatically, and that -T tests the syntax without installing. Added 2026-08-18 (cycle 3, verify-sysadmin-e).

sources.title: anacron(8) — runs commands periodically on machines not running continuously
sources.notes: "Unlike cron(8), it does not assume that the machine is running continuously. Hence, it can be used on machines that are not running 24 hours a day" — the documented reason a cron schedule missed while powered off is not a cron fault. Added 2026-08-18 (cycle 3, verify-sysadmin-e).

sources.title: bootup(7) — system bootup process
sources.notes: States the boot handover order verbatim: firmware does minimal hardware initialisation and hands control to a boot loader, which invokes the kernel, which mounts an initramfs and then the root file system before systemd manages the rest. Added 2026-08-18 (cycle 3, verify-sysadmin-e).

sources.title: systemd-analyze(1) — blame and critical-chain
sources.notes: Documents that blame's ordering "might be misleading as the initialization of one service might be slow simply because it waits for the initialization of another service to complete", and that critical-chain prints the time-critical chain instead. Added 2026-08-18 (cycle 3, verify-sysadmin-e).

sources.title: update-grub(8) — stub for grub-mkconfig (Debian)
sources.notes: "update-grub is a stub for running grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg to generate a grub2 config file" — shipped by the Debian grub2-common package, which is why the command does not exist on Red Hat-family systems. Added 2026-08-18 (cycle 3, verify-sysadmin-e).

sources.title: Configuring kernel command-line parameters / GRUB configuration (RHEL 9)
sources.notes: Shows the Red Hat-family workflow: edit /etc/default/grub, then "Update the GRUB configuration file" with grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg, then reboot for the changes to take effect. Added 2026-08-18 (cycle 3, verify-sysadmin-e).

sources.title: Partitioning (ArchWiki) — GPT versus MBR
sources.notes: "If you are partitioning a disk that is larger than 2 TiB (~2.2 TB), you need to use GPT"; GPT uses 64-bit LBAs while "MBR is limited to addressing 2 TiB of space per drive", and GPT reserves space for 128 partitions by default. Added 2026-08-18 (cycle 3, verify-sysadmin-e).

sources.title: UEFI/Secure Boot (ArchWiki)
sources.notes: "Secure Boot is a security feature found in the UEFI standard" that maintains a signed list of binaries authorised to run at boot, and carries a dedicated "Disabling Secure Boot" procedure — establishing it as one optional UEFI feature rather than a synonym for UEFI. Added 2026-08-18 (cycle 3, verify-sysadmin-e).

sources.title: Configure UEFI/GPT-based hard drive partitions
sources.notes: "On GPT drives, this is known as the EFI System Partition, or the ESP... The device boots to this partition", and a GPT drive may have up to 128 partitions. Added 2026-08-18 (cycle 3, verify-sysadmin-e).

sources.title: runlevel(8) — SysV runlevel to systemd target mapping
sources.notes: Added 2026-08-18 by the System Administration verification pass (task 56, verify-sysadmin-c), which found items citing a source that does not carry the claim. The current systemd.special(7) contains zero occurrences of the word `runlevel`; runlevel(8) carries Table 1, the runlevel-to-target mapping, and the statement that only one runlevel can be active at a time while systemd can activate multiple targets concurrently. freedesktop.org returns 404 for /man/latest/runlevel.html, so the systemd project page is read via man7.org.

sources.title: RFC 1812: Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers
sources.notes: Section 2.1: link-layer packet switching devices are called bridges, and segments joined by bridges share the same IP network prefix forming a single IP subnet. Section 5.3.5.1: "Limited broadcasts MUST NOT be forwarded." Added 2026-08-18 by task 57c: the router-vs-switch items cited RFC 1122, which contains neither statement.

sources.title: RFC 1542: Clarifications and Extensions for the Bootstrap Protocol
sources.notes: Section 4.1.1 specifies BOOTP/DHCP relay agent forwarding; the relaying destination is configurable and may be IP unicast, multicast or broadcast. Added 2026-08-18 by task 57c.

sources.title: RFC 4864: Local Network Protection for IPv6
sources.notes: Abstract: the primary benefit of NAT, amplifying available address space, "is not needed in IPv6"; IPv6 "was designed with the intention of making NAT unnecessary". Section 3.2 covers Unique Local Addresses. Added 2026-08-18 by task 57c: the IPv6-versus-NAT item cited only RFC 3022 and RFC 1918, neither of which mentions IPv6.

sources.title: RFC 5517: Cisco Systems' Private VLANs -- Scalable Security in a Multi-Client Environment
sources.notes: Section 1: "In an Ethernet switch, a VLAN is a broadcast domain in which hosts can establish direct communication with one another at Layer 2." Section 4: ports "can either be access ports or hybrid/trunk ports (according to the terminology presented in Annex D of the IEEE 802.1Q specification)". Added 2026-08-18 by task 57c as a freely readable substitute: the standards.ieee.org 802.1Q page returns 200 but is a catalogue abstract only and carries none of these definitions.

sources.title: RFC 3927: Dynamic Configuration of IPv4 Link-Local Addresses
sources.notes: Defines the 169.254/16 link-local prefix that a host self-configures when no other configuration mechanism, such as DHCP, is available. Added 2026-08-18 by task 57c.

sources.title: getent(1) - get entries from Name Service Switch libraries
sources.notes: getent reads "the Name Service Switch libraries, which are configured in /etc/nsswitch.conf". Added 2026-08-18 by task 57c: the getent-versus-dig item cited nsswitch.conf(5) and hosts(5), neither of which documents getent.

sources.title: nss-resolve(8) - hostname resolution via systemd-resolved.service
sources.notes: Documents the "resolve" nsswitch source: activated by adding "resolve [!UNAVAIL=return]" to the hosts: line, it communicates with systemd-resolved over the Varlink socket /run/systemd/resolve/io.systemd.Resolve, not via the 127.0.0.53 DNS stub, and is recommended before "files" because systemd-resolved supports /etc/hosts internally but with caching. Added 2026-08-18 by task 57c, which refuted an item claiming the resolve module routes lookups through the 127.0.0.53 stub.

sources.title: host(1) - DNS lookup utility
sources.notes: "host is a simple utility for performing DNS lookups. It is normally used to convert names to IP addresses and vice versa." Added 2026-08-18 by task 57c.

sources.title: nslookup(1) - query Internet name servers interactively
sources.notes: "nslookup is a program to query Internet domain name servers. nslookup has two modes: interactive and non-interactive." Added 2026-08-18 by task 57c.

This is the free-to-read PDF of the same Recommendation (47 pages) and it carries the text the OSI items turn on: 6.1.2, 'The Reference Model contains seven layers: a) the Application Layer (layer 7); ... g) the Physical Layer (layer 1).' sources.title: RFC 3021: Using 31-Bit Prefixes on IPv4 Point-to-Point Links
sources.notes: Task 57a: the /31 question named RFC 3021 in its key while citing only RFC 4632 and RFC 791, neither of which mentions /31. Section 2.1: with a 31-bit mask the two resulting addresses 'MUST be interpreted as host addresses', the documented exception to the reserve-network-and-broadcast rule.

sources.title: RFC 6598 / BCP 153: IANA-Reserved IPv4 Prefix for Shared Address Space
sources.notes: Task 57a: the carrier-grade NAT question turned entirely on this document while citing only RFC 1918 and RFC 3022. 'Shared Address Space is distinct from RFC 1918 private address space'; 'The Shared Address Space address range is 100.64.0.0/10.'

sources.title: RFC 4862: IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration
sources.notes: Task 57a: RFC 4291 2.1 requires every interface to have a link-local address, but the mechanism that self-assigns it without any server is specified here, section 5.3 (Creation of Link-Local Addresses). Cited for the fe80:: item's 'configured automatically' claim.

sources.title: RFC 7239: Forwarded HTTP Extension
sources.notes: Section 1 states that proxies make requests appear to originate from the proxy IP address, breaking IP-based logging and access control, and defines the Forwarded header field that restores the original client address.

sources.title: Using nginx as HTTP load balancer
sources.notes: Documents load-balancing methods (round-robin, least-connected, least-time, ip-hash), session persistence via ip_hash, weights, and in-band (passive) server health checks.

sources.title: HAProxy Starter Guide (documentation 3.0)
sources.notes: Section 3 distinguishes packet-level layer 4 load balancing (no content awareness) from layer 7 load balancing on session contents, covers stickiness/persistence, health checking, and the VRRP/keepalived redundancy a load-balancer node itself needs.

sources.title: RFC 5481: Packet Delay Variation Applicability Statement
sources.notes: Section 3.2 explains that real-time (isochronous) applications use a de-jitter buffer sized to the expected delay variation, that too little buffer causes loss and too much harms conversational dynamics.

sources.title: iptables(8) - administration tool for IPv4/IPv6 packet filtering and NAT
sources.notes: TARGETS section: "ACCEPT means to let the packet through.  DROP means to drop the packet on the floor."  -P/--policy sets a built-in chain default policy of ACCEPT or DROP.

sources.title: iptables-extensions(8) - iptables/ip6tables extension modules
sources.notes: Documents the REJECT target ("used to send back an error packet in response to the matched packet: otherwise it is equivalent to DROP", --reject-with icmp-* or tcp-reset) and the conntrack/state matches with NEW, ESTABLISHED and RELATED states.

sources.title: ufw(8) - program for managing a netfilter firewall (Ubuntu manpage)
sources.notes: NOTES: ufw ships disabled with a default incoming policy of deny and stateful tracking for NEW connections. REMOTE MANAGEMENT: ufw enable flushes the chains and "may drop existing connections (eg ssh)"; the documented remedy is to add an allow rule for port 22 before enabling.

sources.title: firewall-cmd(1) - firewalld command line client
sources.notes: Permanent Options: "--permanent ... These changes are not effective immediately, only after service restart/reload or system reboot."  --reload makes the permanent configuration the new runtime configuration and discards runtime-only changes.

sources.title: firewalld.conf(5) - firewalld configuration file
sources.notes: FirewallBackend selects the firewall backend implementation: nftables (default) or iptables - i.e. firewalld drives the kernel netfilter framework.

sources.title: iptables-nft(8) / xtables-nft - iptables using the nftables API
sources.notes: Describes the xtables-nft tools that hook to the nf_tables kernel subsystem via nft_compat and are symlinked in place of the legacy binaries, so /sbin/iptables is normally an nftables front-end; iptables -V reports "(nf_tables)".

sources.title: Nmap Reference Guide: Port Scanning Techniques
sources.notes: SYN scan: "A SYN/ACK indicates the port is listening (open), while a RST (reset) is indicative of a non-listener."  UDP scan: open and filtered ports rarely send any response, while closed UDP ports usually return an ICMP port unreachable.

sources.title: hostname(1) — show or set the system's host name
sources.notes: Documents the -f/--fqdn flag and states that the FQDN is whatever the resolver returns for the host name, changed via /etc/hosts when hosts is the first lookup method. Added 2026-08-18 by task 57d.

sources.title: hostname(5) — local hostname configuration file
sources.notes: HOSTNAME SEMANTICS section defines the static hostname in /etc/hostname and the transient hostname set at runtime, for example from a DHCP lease, with static taking priority. Added 2026-08-18 by task 57d.

sources.title: RFC 2181: Clarifications to the DNS Specification
sources.notes: Section 10.1 states the exhaustive CNAME coexistence rule; section 8 clarifies TTL as an unsigned maximum time to live. Added 2026-08-18 by task 57d.

sources.title: RFC 2308: Negative Caching of DNS Queries (DNS NCACHE)
sources.notes: Replaces RFC 1034 section 4.3.4. Sections 5 and 6 define the negative-cache TTL as the minimum of SOA.MINIMUM and the SOA TTL, and require cached answers to be returned with the TTL decremented by their time in cache. Added 2026-08-18 by task 57d.

sources.title: Kea Administrator Reference Manual: The DHCPv4 Server
sources.notes: Sections 8.3.1 and 8.3.2 document in-pool versus out-of-pool host reservations and how the server resolves a reservation that conflicts with an existing dynamic lease. ISC DHCP (dhcpd) is end-of-life; Kea is its maintained successor. Added 2026-08-18 by task 57d.

sources.title: Ubuntu Server documentation: Firewalls
sources.notes: "The Linux kernel includes the netfilter subsystem ... All modern Linux firewall solutions use this system for packet filtering" and "The default firewall configuration tool for Ubuntu is ufw."

sources.title: Fedora Quick Docs: Using firewalld
sources.notes: "All Fedora Editions install, configure and activate the firewall by default" via firewalld; also states that changes made while firewalld is running are lost on restart, when settings revert to their permanent values.

sources.title: RFC 8499: DNS Terminology
sources.notes: Definitional source for DNS terms. Defines fully-qualified domain name against partially qualified names, and records that "host name" is not defined in RFC 1034, RFC 1035, RFC 1123 or RFC 2181. Added 2026-08-18 by task 57d.
